title: GeoJSON Simplify Helper: Lighten Heavy Polygons
description: Simplify heavy GeoJSON polygons in your browser with the GeoJSON Simplify Helper — see vertex counts, set tolerance, download the lighter file. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a coastline polygon carrying 40,000 vertices can shed most of them at a 0.001-degree tolerance — about 111 metres of allowed wiggle — and stay visibly the same coastline at map zoom.
quick_answer: The GeoJSON Simplify Helper loads detailed GeoJSON polygons in your browser, shows how complex they are, and simplifies the geometry so heavy files get lighter. Drop a file, check the vertex counts, choose a tolerance, and download a copy whose shapes survive at map scale while the byte count falls.

Dashboards and map platforms cap file sizes. Simplification is the honest way under the cap — deleting features is not.
Every vertex is battery and bandwidth on a phone in the field. A simplified copy is the field edition of the same geography.
Sometimes the shock is the diagnosis: one polygon holds 90% of the vertices. The counts this helper shows point at the culprit feature.

A tolerance of 0.001 degrees allows features to move up to about 111 metres; 0.0001 degrees, about 11 metres. Choose by the smallest feature you must keep — a river bend narrower than the tolerance is a bend the simplifier may erase.

body.t: If a 2 MB file drops to a few hundred KB after simplification with the map unchanged at viewing zoom, the vertices were resolution the screen could never show. That gap — file truth versus screen truth — is the helper's whole subject.

popular_table.title: What simplification actually does
popular_table.intro: The Douglas–Peucker idea in plain words — the algorithm this helper implements.
rows: A straight line between a line's endpoints
Its perpendicular distance from the chord
Drop every vertex between — the chord represents them
Keep that vertex, split the line, repeat on both halves
popular_table.note: Simplification removes vertices; it never moves the ones it keeps. Kept points stay exactly on the original geometry — the shape thins, it does not drift.

faq: Douglas–Peucker (1973), the standard line-simplification method: recursively keep the vertex farthest from each chord until every dropped point lies within the tolerance of the simplified line.
Simplifying polygon rings can occasionally create self-intersections at aggressive tolerances. Validate the output with the GeoJSON Validator and lower the tolerance if a ring misbehaves.
Does it simplify points and properties?
Points have nothing to thin — the helper's work is lines and polygon rings. Properties ride along untouched on the features that carry them.

Smaller than your smallest must-keep feature, in degrees: 0.0001° ≈ 11 m for detailed work, 0.001° ≈ 111 m for overview maps. Start low; you can always simplify the original harder, never the copy finer.

GeoJSON coordinates are degrees, so the tolerance speaks degrees. The metre equivalents on this page (≈111 m per 0.001° of latitude) help you choose; longitude degrees shrink toward the poles, as everywhere on this site.
Can it create gaps between neighbouring polygons?

Yes — shared borders simplified independently can diverge by up to the tolerance, opening slivers. For interlocking boundaries (counties, parcels), topology-aware tools (TopoJSON workflows) are the professional answer.
Does simplifying change area and length?
Yes, slightly — removed wiggles were real length. Report measurements from the original file; publish the simplified one for display.
